Geology
The Tract II and Tract III lease areas of Westmoreland Resources are at the western margin of surface exposure of the Tongue River member of the Fort Union formation, in the northwest part of the Powder River basin. The tract areas are entirely underlain by non-marine strata of the Fort Union formation of Paleocene age. Dip of the beds is less than one degree to the Northeast.
When the inland seas of the Cretaceous period receded about 70 million years ago a coastal plain with only minor relief was formed. This plain became the site of deposition for the Hell Creek formation, youngest of the Cretaceous strata (Table II-7).
Slight warping of the old ocean floor and coastal plains created broad shallow basins. Sediments were eroded from the rising mountain ranges to the west and began to fill the basins. There were intermittent quiescent periods during which thick intervals of vegetational growth were deposited. These buried organic strata were eventually transformed into coal. The oldest of these basin sediments is the Fort Union formation. The uppermost member of the Fort Union, the Tongue River, contains most of the coal seams of economic value.
Continued warping of the basins of deposition imparted some warping to the originally flat layers of sediment that were deposited in the basins. Their eroded margins now outline the basins with concentric bands of outcropping sedimentary layers.
